subject: Signals and Systems

questions.text: Define energy signal and power signal with mathematical expressions and examples. Determine whether the signal $x(t) = e^{-at}u(t)$ for $a > 0$ (or $x(t) = 5\cos(t)$) is an energy signal, power signal, or neither, and calculate its total energy or average power.

Show that any arbitrary continuous or discrete time signal can be decomposed into an even component and an odd component ($x(t) = x_e(t) + x_o(t)$). Find and sketch the even and odd components of a given signal.
Explain time shifting, time scaling, and time reversal (reflection) operations on continuous-time and discrete-time signals with neat graphical illustrations.
Derive the necessary condition for a discrete-time complex exponential signal $x[n] = e^{j\omega_0 n}$ to be periodic. What is its fundamental period $N$?
State and prove Parseval's relation for: (a) Continuous-Time Fourier Series, and (b) Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS).
Find the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT) of the signal $x(t) = e^{-at}u(t)$ for $a > 0$. Plot its magnitude and phase spectrum.
State and prove the Convolution property of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform: $\mathcal{F}\{x_1(t) * x_2(t)\} = X_1(j\omega) X_2(j\omega)$.
State and prove the Duality property and Time-Scaling property of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform.
Derive the Convolution Integral for a continuous-time Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) system: $y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau$.

Derive the Convolution Sum for a discrete-time LTI system: $y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty x[k]h[n-k]$. Find and plot the convolution sum of sequences $x[n] = \{1, 3, 4, 3, 1\}$ and $h[n] = \{2, 2, -2\}$ (or $x[n] = \{3, 1, 5\}$ and $h[n] = \{1, 4, -2, 3\}$).

Define an LTI system and explain fundamental system properties: Linearity, Time-Invariance, Causality, Memory, and BIBO Stability. State the condition for an LTI system to be causal and stable in terms of impulse response.

State and prove the Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem using frequency-domain analysis. Define Nyquist rate and Nyquist interval. What is aliasing and how is it prevented? Determine the Nyquist rate for $x(t) = \cos(200\pi t) + \sin(400\pi t)$.

Derive formula to calculate the impulse response of an Ideal Low-Pass Filter in continuous/discrete time. Prove, with necessary mathematical derivations, that an ideal low-pass filter is non-causal and physically unrealizable.
Derive the synthesis and analysis equations of the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT). State and prove the Linearity, Time-Shifting, and Frequency-Shifting properties of DTFT.
Compute the 4-point Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for the sequence $x[n] = \{3, -2, 1, 4\}$ using the twiddle factor matrix $W_N^{kn}$.
For a system characterized by a linear constant coefficient difference equation, determine the frequency response $H(e^{j\omega})$ and impulse response $h[n]$. Plot the magnitude and phase response.

Define the Continuous-Time Convolution Integral $y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau) h(t - \tau) d\tau$. Compute the analytical and graphical convolution of two rectangular pulses $x(t) = u(t) - u(t - 2)$ and $h(t) = u(t) - u(t - 3)$.
questions.solutionOutline: Convolution computes zero-state response of LTI system to arbitrary input. Flip and shift h(t - tau). Intervals of overlap: for t < 0, y(t) = 0; for 0 <= t < 2, y(t) = integral_0^t 1 d tau = t; for 2 <= t < 3, overlap is full duration 2, y(t) = 2; for 3 <= t < 5, overlap from t-3 to 2, y(t) = 5 - t; for t >= 5, y(t) = 0. Produces trapezoidal pulse response.

questions.text: State and prove the Dirichlet Conditions for the existence and convergence of Fourier Series. Determine the Continuous-Time Fourier Series (CTFS) exponential coefficients $c_n$ for a periodic symmetric square wave and plot its line spectrum.
questions.solutionOutline: Dirichlet conditions: 1) Absolutely integrable over one period: integral |x(t)| dt < infty; 2) Finite number of maxima and minima within one period; 3) Finite number of finite discontinuities. For square wave with period T and amplitude A: c_n = (1/T) integral_{-T/4}^{T/4} A e^(-j n omega_0 t) dt = (A / n pi) sin(n pi / 2) = (2A / n pi) for n = 1, 5, 9... and -(2A / n pi) for n = 3, 7... Sinc envelope line spectrum.

questions.text: State and prove key properties of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT): Time-Shifting, Frequency-Shifting (Modulation), Time-Scaling, and Duality Property. Compute the Fourier transform of a Gaussian pulse $x(t) = e^{-a t^2}$.
questions.solutionOutline: Time-shift: x(t - t0) <-> X(omega) e^(-j omega t0). Frequency shift: x(t) e^(j omega_0 t) <-> X(omega - omega_0). Time scaling: x(a t) <-> (1/|a|) X(omega / a). Duality: X(t) <-> 2 pi x(-omega). For Gaussian x(t) = exp(-a t^2): complete square in exponent: X(omega) = integral exp(-a t^2 - j omega t) dt = sqrt(pi / a) exp(-omega^2 / 4a), proving Gaussian transform is also Gaussian.

questions.text: State and prove Parseval's Theorem for Continuous-Time Energy and Power Signals. For signal $x(t) = e^{-a t} u(t)$ ($a > 0$), calculate the total energy in the time domain and verify using frequency domain energy spectral density $|X(\omega)|^2$.
questions.solutionOutline: Parseval theorem states energy E = integral_{-infty}^{infty} |x(t)|^2 dt = (1/2 pi) integral_{-infty}^{infty} |X(omega)|^2 d omega. For e^(-at) u(t): time-domain E = integral_0^infty e^(-2at) dt = 1/(2a). In frequency domain: X(omega) = 1/(a + j omega) => |X(omega)|^2 = 1/(a^2 + omega^2). Energy E = (1/2 pi) integral_{-infty}^{infty} d omega / (a^2 + omega^2) = (1/2 pi) * (pi / a) = 1/(2a). Exactly verified.

questions.text: Explain Ideal Lowpass Filter and Paley-Wiener Criterion for filter physical realizability. Prove that an ideal brick-wall lowpass filter is non-causal and exhibits the Gibbs phenomenon in its step response.
questions.solutionOutline: Paley-Wiener theorem: for causal filter, frequency response must satisfy integral_{-infty}^infty |ln|H(omega)|| / (1 + omega^2) d omega < infty. Ideal brick-wall filter has H(omega) = 0 for |omega| > omega_c, making integral diverge (-infty), so it is physically unrealizable. Impulse response h(t) = (omega_c / pi) sinc(omega_c t) exists for all t < 0 (non-causal). Step response truncation produces Gibbs phenomenon 8.95% overshoot at discontinuity.

questions.text: Explain the Sampling Theorem for low-pass and band-pass signals. What is Aliasing? Explain Flat-top sampling and the derivation of aperture distortion with equalizer reconstruction.
questions.solutionOutline: Continuous signal can be uniquely recovered if sampled at rate f_s >= 2 f_max. Flat-top sampling models pulse train convolved with rectangular aperture p(t) of width tau. Spectrum X_s(f) = (1/T_s) P(f) sum X(f - k f_s), where P(f) = tau sinc(f tau). The sinc roll-off attenuates high frequencies within baseband (aperture effect / high-frequency roll-off). Compensated by equalization filter with response 1 / sinc(f tau).

questions.text: Define the Bilateral Laplace Transform and Region of Convergence (ROC). Derive properties of ROC for causal, anti-causal, and two-sided signals. Determine the Laplace transform and ROC of $x(t) = e^{-2t} u(t) + e^{-3t} u(-t)$.
questions.solutionOutline: X(s) = integral_{-infty}^infty x(t) e^(-st) dt, s = sigma + j omega. ROC consists of vertical strips in s-plane containing no poles. For causal signal (right-sided), ROC is Re(s) > max(Re(poles)). For anti-causal (left-sided), ROC is Re(s) < min(Re(poles)). For e^(-2t) u(t), pole at s = -2, ROC: Re(s) > -2. For e^(-3t) u(-t), pole at s = -3, ROC: Re(s) < -3. Intersection of ROCs is empty set (Re(s) > -2 and Re(s) < -3 has no overlap); hence Laplace transform does not exist.

questions.text: Solve the differential equation $\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} + 5\frac{dy}{dt} + 6y(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} + x(t)$ for unit step input $x(t) = u(t)$ with initial conditions $y(0^-) = 1, y'(0^-) = 2$ using the unilateral Laplace transform, separating Zero-Input and Zero-State responses.
questions.solutionOutline: Unilateral transform: L{y'} = s Y(s) - y(0^-); L{y''} = s^2 Y(s) - s y(0^-) - y'(0^-). Substituting gives (s^2 + 5s + 6) Y(s) - s - 7 = (s + 1)/s. Y(s) = [s + 7]/(s+2)(s+3) [Zero-Input Response] + [s + 1]/s(s+2)(s+3) [Zero-State Response]. Partial fractions yield y_zi(t) = (5 e^(-2t) - 4 e^(-3t)) u(t) and y_zs(t) = (1/6 - 0.5 e^(-2t) + 1/3 e^(-3t)) u(t). Total y(t) = y_zi + y_zs.

questions.text: Define the Discrete-Time Convolution Sum $y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k] h[n - k]$. Compute the convolution of $x[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]$ and $h[n] = u[n] - u[n - 4]$.

Define the Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT). State its properties and compute the frequency response $H(e^{j\Omega})$ and magnitude response $|H(e^{j\Omega})|$ of an LTI system described by difference equation $y[n] - 0.5 y[n-1] = x[n]$.
questions.solutionOutline: DTFT X(Omega) = sum x[n] e^(-j Omega n); periodic in Omega with period 2 pi. Taking DTFT of difference equation: Y(Omega)(1 - 0.5 e^(-j Omega)) = X(Omega). Frequency response H(e^(j Omega)) = 1 / (1 - 0.5 e^(-j Omega)). Magnitude |H| = 1 / sqrt(1.25 - cos Omega). At Omega=0, |H|=2 (lowpass peak); at Omega=pi, |H|=1/1.5=0.67.

questions.text: Determine the System Function $H(z)$, pole-zero constellation, impulse response $h[n]$, and BIBO stability for a discrete LTI system given by $y[n] - \frac{3}{4} y[n-1] + \frac{1}{8} y[n-2] = x[n] + 2 x[n-1]$.
questions.solutionOutline: Z-transform yields H(z) = (1 + 2 z^(-1)) / (1 - 0.75 z^(-1) + 0.125 z^(-2)) = (1 + 2 z^(-1)) / [(1 - 0.5 z^(-1))(1 - 0.25 z^(-1))]. Poles at z = 0.5 and z = 0.25; zero at z = -2. Both poles lie strictly inside unit circle (|z| < 1), so causal ROC |z| > 0.5 contains unit circle, proving system is BIBO stable. Partial fractions give h[n] = [10 (0.5)^n - 9 (0.25)^n] u[n].

questions.text: Explain System Properties: Linearity, Time-Invariance, Memory, Causality, and Invertibility. Test whether the following systems satisfy linearity and time-invariance: (a) $y(t) = x(2t)$, (b) $y(t) = t x(t)$, (c) $y[n] = x^2[n]$.
questions.solutionOutline: (a) y(t) = x(2t): Linear (superposition holds), but Time-Variant (delaying input gives x(2t - 2t0) != y(t - t0) = x(2(t - t0))). (b) y(t) = t x(t): Linear, but Time-Variant due to explicit t multiplier. (c) y[n] = x^2[n]: Time-Invariant, but Non-Linear because (a x1 + b x2)^2 != a x1^2 + b x2^2.

questions.text: Explain the relationship and mapping between Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT), Laplace Transform, Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT), and Z-Transform.
questions.solutionOutline: Laplace transform evaluates signals over entire complex s = sigma + j omega plane; CTFT is special case of Laplace evaluated strictly on imaginary axis s = j omega (valid if ROC contains j-omega axis). Z-transform evaluates discrete signals over complex z = r e^(j Omega) plane; DTFT is Z-transform evaluated on unit circle |z| = 1. Continuous to discrete mapping uses z = e^(s T).

questions.text: Define Group Delay $\tau_g(\omega) = -\frac{d\theta(\omega)}{d\omega}$ and Phase Delay $\tau_p(\omega) = -\frac{\theta(\omega)}{\omega}$. Explain how non-linear phase response causes dispersion and waveform distortion in broadband communication channels.
questions.solutionOutline: Phase delay is time delay experienced by single frequency sinusoidal component. Group delay is time delay of signal envelope (wave packet) comprising narrow band of frequencies. If phase response theta(omega) is linear (theta = -omega t0), then tau_p = tau_g = t0 = constant (distortionless transmission). Non-linear phase causes different frequency components to arrive at different times, causing phase dispersion and pulse broadening.
